source.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
facts: In Anthropic’s internal research evaluation, an Opus 4 lead with Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2 percent.
Anthropic usage data reports about four times chat tokens for agents and about fifteen times for multi-agent systems.
Complex queries can take up to 90 percent less time when independent paths run in parallel.
Tasks with heavy shared context or dependencies, including many coding tasks, often fit a single agent better.

centralThesis: Multi-agent is not a default upgrade but a fit-and-economics decision: parallelism pays when a valuable task splits into independent paths and one context or tool budget becomes the bottleneck.
reusableArtifact: Single-vs-multi-agent decision tree: independent paths, context pressure, result value, delegation contract, effort tier, evaluation, and recovery.

chapters.title: Pass the fit gate
chapters.promise: The first move is not adding agents. It is deciding whether the problem contains independent exploration paths that deserve parallel work.

recaps.narration: Chapter recap. First, look for paths that can progress independently.
Second, be cautious when the task depends on heavily shared state.
Third, reserve the higher cost for high-value outcomes.

chapters.title: Write a delegation contract
chapters.promise: After the fit gate, the lead agent’s main job is not searching. It is dividing the question into assignments that do not overlap and do not leave gaps.

recaps.narration: Chapter recap. First, make the objective and output explicit.
Second, specify sources, tools, and boundaries together.
Third, collect evidence and uncertainty, not conclusions alone.

chapters.title: Size the effort
chapters.promise: Multi-agent does not mean more is always better. Search effort should scale with both question complexity and expected value.

recaps.narration: Chapter recap. First, choose an effort tier from task complexity.
Second, parallel gains come from overlapping independent waits.
Third, stop expanding when marginal value starts to fall.

chapters.title: Evaluate quality
chapters.promise: Multi-agent paths change dynamically, so evaluation cannot require one fixed sequence of steps.

recaps.narration: Chapter recap. First, evaluate facts, citations, and coverage.
Second, allow dynamic paths but require an explainable process.
Third, use a real baseline to decide whether parallelism pays.
recaps.screenText: Use a baseline to judge value

chapters.title: Build for recovery
chapters.promise: A research demo that finishes once is not yet a multi-agent system that can recover reliably in production.

recaps.narration: Chapter recap. First, persist state and evidence outside the process.
Second, retry only the failed path and preserve the full trace.
Third, protect production with gradual releases and stopping rules.

factBoundaries: The 90.2 percent result is an internal Anthropic research evaluation, not a universal performance promise.
The four-times and fifteen-times token figures describe Anthropic usage patterns, not fixed costs for every implementation.
Agent counts and tool-call ranges are examples from Anthropic’s research system, not mandatory settings.
inference: The single-vs-multi-agent decision tree is an applied synthesis of the source, not an official Anthropic template.
